prose_changes.old: Pietism grew out of Lutheran devotion together with the influence of Dutch Reformed precisianism, and gave rise in turn to the Moravian Church and the wider Protestant missionary movement. prose_changes.new: Pietism grew out of Lutheran devotion. Spener's Pia Desideria first came out as a preface to a book of sermons by Johann Arndt. Pietism may also owe something to the strict Dutch Reformed piety called precisianism. But no early Pietist text we hold names a Dutch source. Pietism shaped the Moravian Church at Herrnhut, and it sent some of the first Protestant missions out of Europe. Pietism in Württemberg, linked with Johann Albrecht Bengel, belongs to this same movement.
prose_changes.reason: 'Gave rise in turn to the Moravian Church' overstates: the Herrnhut refugees came from the old Unity, and Pietism reached them through Zinzendorf (now the influenced link). 'The influence of Dutch Reformed precisianism' is stated as fact, but no vendored Pietist text names a Dutch source, so it is qualified with the reason. 'Gave rise to the wider Protestant missionary movement' becomes 'sent some of the first Protestant missions out of Europe', the entry's own claim and supported by Guericke on Tranquebar. The Lutheran root is kept and now shown: Pia Desideria began as a preface to Arndt's postil. Old field scored FRE 27; whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: Pietism never became a denomination of its own — it stayed inside the Lutheran churches and eventually dissolved as a distinct party — but almost everything it touched outlived it. The Moravians at Herrnhut came out of its orbit and through them John Wesley; the Protestant missionary movement's first sustained institutional base was at Halle. And the Halle foundations themselves are still standing and still working in Saxony-Anhalt, orphanage buildings, library, cabinet of curiosities and all. Its habits — small groups meeting midweek to read Scripture, and the expectation that a Christian can tell the story of their own conversion — are now so ordinary across evangelical Protestantism that their origin is easy to miss.
prose_changes.new: Pietism never became a church of its own. It stayed inside the Lutheran churches and in time faded as a separate party. But almost everything it touched outlived it. The Moravians at Herrnhut grew up close to it. Their patron, Count Zinzendorf, was Spener's godson and went to school at Halle. John Wesley learned from the Moravians, and in 1738 he went to Halle himself. George Whitefield took Francke's orphan house as the model for his own in Georgia. Halle also chose and backed the first missionaries the king of Denmark sent to India, in 1706. The Halle foundations still stand and still work in Saxony-Anhalt: the orphanage buildings, the library, the cabinet of curiosities and all. Its habits are now so ordinary across evangelical Protestantism that their origin is easy to miss. Small groups meet midweek to read Scripture. A Christian is expected to tell the story of their own conversion.
prose_changes.reason: 'Through them John Wesley' is replaced by what the sources show: Wesley learned from the Moravians and also went to Halle himself in 1738; Whitefield modeled his Georgia orphan house on Francke's (both in the new influenced link). The unsupported superlative 'the Protestant missionary movement's first sustained institutional base was at Halle' becomes Halle's documented role in choosing and backing the 1706 Danish mission (Guericke). Zinzendorf's Spener and Halle ties are added to carry the Moravian link. Every other fact kept; the old field scored FRE 27 and FK 16.5, so it is rewritten whole in shorter sentences.

prose_changes.old: This community is a direct renewal of the old Bohemian Unity of the Brethren, carried across the hidden century between its suppression in 1627 and the refugees' arrival at Herrnhut in 1722. Its episcopal succession was renewed through the Jablonski-Nitschmann consecration of 1735, tying it formally back to the old Unity. It had a decisive influence on John Wesley, and began sending missionaries decades before any other Protestant body did.
prose_changes.new: This community saw itself as the old Bohemian Unity of the Brethren made new. In its own telling, the Unity was suppressed in 1627 and survived in hiding for a century. Then its refugees reached Herrnhut in 1722. In 1735 the old Unity's senior bishop, Daniel Ernst Jablonski, made David Nitschmann a bishop. That tied the new church formally to the old one. Yet its patron, Count Zinzendorf, was a Lutheran Pietist. At first he meant Herrnhut as a gathering inside the Lutheran church. It had a deep effect on John Wesley. From 1732 it sent missionaries far overseas.
prose_changes.reason: 'A direct renewal of the old Bohemian Unity' presents the community's own reading as settled; the continued-as link is Contested, since Zinzendorf first meant Herrnhut as a Lutheran Pietist gathering (Spangenberg). Now framed as the community's own view, with the other side stated. 'Began sending missionaries decades before any other Protestant body did' is wrong: Halle's Danish mission reached Tranquebar in 1706 (the Pietism entry's own text; Guericke), 26 years before 1732. Now 'from 1732 it sent missionaries far overseas'. The Jablonski-Nitschmann consecration is kept and spelled out from Cranz. Old field scored FRE 27; rewritten whole.

prose_changes.old: The Moravian Church is a living worldwide body, and far larger outside Europe than in it. The great majority of its members are in Tanzania and the Caribbean, the long fruit of the mission work begun in 1732. Its most consequential single contact was with a young Anglican priest: John Wesley met Moravians in a storm at sea and again in London, and the Methodist revival carries their fingerprints. The Losungen, a book of daily Scripture texts drawn by lot at Herrnhut and printed every year since 1731, is still published and read in dozens of languages. One of the longest unbroken publishing runs in the world. And the hidden-seed story ended well: a church suppressed in Bohemia in 1627 has descendants in every continent.
